column2: The following year, Alvin Charles Few's school holds a fair one evening; Malrey, June, Vera, and Mary go. In the fortune-telling booth, the fortune-teller reads her palm and predicts several miscarriages; comparing notes, the white women discover that she gave each of them the same prediction. Mary admires the fortune-teller's subtle social reading. fair booths, a palm, a prediction of miscarriages

Peter Nemenyi, who studied physics with Max Dehn, leaves for Princeton around 1950. Farewells with embraces in front of North Lodge: his car goes down the road; a living identity went out of his life that day. The school adjusts to his loss as to a missing vital organ, but he had to go. The exact spot: in front of North Lodge, facing the dinner gong and the back entrance of the Dining Hall; embraces with Nick and Herb. Consequences: Dawson senses that he is the next to leave.

After a few weeks in Provincetown, Frankenthaler goes south: first to her New York roommate, the actress Gaby Rodgers, at the Abington Theater, then to Black Mountain to see Clem Greenberg, teaching there for the summer. She makes many works on paper during this short stay. Rationed electricity: flashlights and candles; venomous snakes slithering across the road at night, visible by flashlight; gasoline scarce, cars hard to find. Consequences: The snakes dissuade her from staying longer (she is not much of a camper, she says).

A “luxury” outing by car to a summit to dine and listen to jazz: the blind pianist George Shearing, behind his dark glasses, sang songs of a polished elegance compared with BMC nights. The blind pianist's dark glasses.

Drinks at the end of the day in Clem's office; a photo (kept by Frankenthaler) shows Theodore Stamos sitting on the floor and Clem at his desk; another snapshot, taken by Cora Ward, it seems, shows Clem and Helen at the natural swimming hole, their heads under the waterfall. Cherished photographs; a swimming hole with a waterfall.

A verse play with a chorus and jazz music: Mark, tangled in party streamers, weeps, frees himself, and discovers behind the noise a night alive with millions of tentative movements. The party evoked: a party house built inside the house by Don Alter, after Mondrian, with transparent striped walls. Loud jazz punctuating the silences; colored streamers; strong punch; an untiring trumpet; striped walls after Mondrian showing the dancers striped with red and with space; characters named Anderson, Sally, Diana. Consequences: A play connected with the 1950 summer session (Goodman, “Faculty 1950 SS”).

A room is decorated with colored papers, with a house within the house built by Don Alter after Mondrian; people dance through the striped walls, the trumpet plays endlessly, the punch is strong; the streamers get tangled, dancers fall, couples and jealousies are reshuffled colored papers, red-and-white striped walls, trumpet, punch, multicolored streamers; Harvey and Virginia leave the room; Mark dances with Mary Carolyn while Harold dances with Sally Consequences: a haunted night for the narrator Mark after the party

Forbes draws up a list of candidates but fails: the post pays 90 dollars a month, its powers are undefined, with no guarantee of tenure. The very title of “rector” is troubling (most people think first of a church); Forbes suggests “president” for the negotiations. In the spring, he returns the letters and the last names to the college and leaves for Europe. 90 dollars a month; the title changed to “president”

The Board votes against reappointing M.C. Richards; for her, an absolute thunderbolt. In reality the vote is aimed at Levi: as his wife, she is lumped together with him in a single package, the traditionalist assumption being that the wife leaves with the husband. Others, however, had criticized the traditionalists' plans: Leser, Hazel Larsen, Flola Shepard, sometimes even Natasha. Consequences: Three months of battle, dozens of meetings and votes

Nick Cernovich, the Student Moderator, organizes a student poll: a large majority for reappointing all three. Most of the teachers not on the Board share M.C.'s indignation. A joke: Black Mountain, the only college where students come back year after year to welcome the new teachers Consequences: The faculty recommends rehiring all three; the Board reverses its decision; M.C. reappointed almost immediately

Flola Shepard has to speak to Fiore about the “irregularity” of his life; he agrees to moderate his displays of affection until his divorce. An interference inherited from the New England-Germanic climate, unthinkable a year later.

A student asks to borrow his copy of Lady Chatterley's Lover; Levi replies acidly that he no longer dares lend it to him since the scandal, because people will say he is corrupting the morals of youth.

Separate motions to recall Corkran, Trayer, and Warrington from the Board and to add a ninth member to break the tie. Flola Shepard and Paul Leser defend Levi (a shared leftist orientation; they see the educational conservatives as political conservatives: Corkran defends American capitalism, Natasha, a White Russian, denounces communism). Others side with Levi on principle or out of distrust of Natasha's zeal to clear the ground. Consequences: Reappointment obtained; Corkran resigns as registrar and Board member, saying he is more representative of the dominant opinions and forces

A wide net of invitations, on an equal footing, with suggestions from Cage, Olson, Cunningham, and de Kooning (all invited back, but all engaged elsewhere). Acceptances: Goodman (writing), Greenberg (art history and criticism), Stamos (painting). Additions: Katherine Litz (dance, recruited by Betty Jennerjahn; she had danced with Humphrey-Weidman and with Agnes de Mille and taught at the New York YMHA), Leo Amino (sculpture), Robert Klein (theater; a long career as a director and producer in Berlin and London). Terms: room and board, $160 in cash, up to $100 in travel expenses Consequences: The “homosexual summer” of 1950, final proof for the conservatives of moral disintegration

At student meetings on the Goodman question, a navy veteran complains that Goodman urinated in public — he had in fact peed behind a tree during a softball game, the restrooms being far from the field. Oppenheimer compares this to the old lady in the hotel who complained of a naked man and suggested that the clerk climb onto the dresser to get a better view. Consequences: A student majority for Goodman, but a decision that was long and dirty, according to Dan Rice, allowing the faculty to invoke dissent

Levi's defense of Goodman, combined with a remark suggesting that the farm be given up if it kept losing money, sends Trayer into such a rage that he hits Levi in the middle of a meeting. A loud thud: Levi gets up from the floor rubbing his jaw. Oppenheimer jumps on Trayer's back, yelling “You fucking bastard!”; Johanna Jalowetz eggs him on from the sidelines: “You tell him!”. Goodman nicknames Oppenheimer “The Wild Bull of the Campus”. Levi, laconic, will tell Flola Shepard he had no idea the occupation of teaching was so hazardous. Levi: “I had no idea... the occupation of teaching was so hazardous”; Oppenheimer: “You fucking bastard!”

The faculty overwhelmingly rejects the invitation for him to stay for the regular year. The Quaker bloc: a threat to their children; Max Dehn, not antihomosexual, thinks that Goodman's rhetoric of freedom denies the real freedom of adolescents, persuaded by his eloquence rather than by their own choice. Defenders: does Paul want your thirteen-year-old boy when there are all these groovy twenty-year-olds?; an intensely moral man; Levi: a reasonable price to pay for his genius. Even homosexual summer teachers are wary of his acting out. A fear expressed that he would rape their thirteen-year-old children; a rumor of a required course in homosexuality for the 17-18-year-old boys Consequences: Goodman does not stay; six months later he would have had a more favorable hearing, a year later the hearing would have been laughed at, two years later he would have been hired

According to Corkran, the candidates for rector were “rundown crocks of the southern educational establishment,” with the exception of Carleton Washburne, a professor of education at Brooklyn College, who withdraws his candidacy on realizing that the post would have made him the faculty's handyman. Huss's acceptance leads Corkran to give up his own departure: with a solid man, it is worth holding on a little longer. Corkran's phrase: “rundown crocks of the southern educational establishment” Consequences: Huss becomes rector

Betty Jennerjahn pleads passionately for Joe and Mary (Levi), but Pete Jennerjahn votes against Levi's reelection. Believing that Betty, who personally dislikes Levi, would vote as he did, he then incurs her anger: no one, she says, should be driven out of Black Mountain out of personal dislike. Consequences: The departure of Bill Levi and, with him, of Natasha

An additional and perhaps decisive reason for Natasha's departure: her marriage to an older student. Because of the McCarthyite witch hunt, she then has great difficulty finding work. Consequences: Lasting professional difficulties after BMC
Huss accepts the offer of the post of rector only after five visits to the community. 5 visits

Just before Levi leaves, Huss offers to take him to dinner and asks whom he would like to invite; Levi answers “Natasha” — the very person who had so long led the effort to purge him. Dan Rice comments: that's the philosopher in him.

At 18, his father, with his mother's silent assent, throws him out of the house for not going to church and for homosexuality; he rents a room at $7 a week behind Independence Hall and works in a factory. $7 a week, a semi-red-light district of Philadelphia Consequences: Early independence and precariousness

Just after high school, working to pay for Rider College, Rumaker climbs to the top of the mast of a tanker in dry dock with his mask, his grinder, and yards of air hose, to grind a wide oval on a shaky scaffold a foot wide; he panics, and his boss advises him not to look down and climbs down ahead of him. a view of Camden and South Philly beyond the muddy Delaware, a plank a foot wide Consequences: This advice will serve again in the silo in 1952

Merrill waits for Rumaker at the kitchen door, takes him to his shack, slowly undresses him, lays him down on the bare mattress near the stove; mutual oral sex, Rumaker's first time; a simultaneous climax that Rumaker takes as a good omen; he then goes back to South Lodge without staying a bare mattress on the floor, a nearby stove, a worn plaid wool shirt, milky skin, pepper-and-salt / light brown hair, a lean, muscular body, a musky smell, a swampy scent like the marshes in summer Consequences: The beginning of the affair; Rumaker almost never sleeps in the South Lodge attic dormitory all winter

Told in the spring of 1953 on the dining hall porch: Olson used to read the tarot for anyone who asked him; having divined a student's suicide, he prudently concealed it from him; learning a year later (1950) that the student had indeed killed himself, he gave up the cards forever. Consequences: The tarot abandoned for good.

Elaine will later say that a long binge began in 1950 and still holds parts of the art world in its grip; it springs as much from the smell of success as from alcohol: fame and money seem imminent, everything seems possible. Consequences: The collective euphoria of the Abstract Expressionists.

De Kooning exhibits with Baziotes, Gottlieb, Hofmann, Motherwell, Tobey, and Tomlin in Black on White: Paintings by European and American Artists. Consequences: A debate over who, de Kooning or Pollock, first adopted the black-and-white palette (Gorky, Tworkov, Motherwell, Brooks, Kline also cited)

From the 1950s on, Elaine drank regularly from the morning (a little something in the coffee), all day and in the evening; for a long time she refused to call herself an alcoholic while acknowledging that she was one, like almost the whole scene.

The material of the book, given as an assignment in a standard psychology course, was tried out on students. At one of the universities, ages ranged from 18 to nearly 70, and many worked part-time or full-time. Written reports collected over four months (the length of the term). The second time, more students; nearly a hundred permissions to use their reports anonymously. Follow-ups show that the development begun continues at an accelerated pace after the course. 18 to 70 years old; four months; nearly a hundred permissions to quote Consequences: Confirmation that therapy can be reduced to a reader alone with printed instructions

Goodman discovers in class that his students have never read the Bible, Milton, Dryden, Gibbon, etc., and above all that they do not feel the existence of these works as a lack; on the other hand, they know odd facts about Mayan hieroglyphics, a subject that interested their teacher. Authors never read: the Bible, Milton, Dryden, Gibbon; fragmentary knowledge: “odd facts about Mayan hieroglyphics”. Consequences: Goodman sees in this a sign that these young people, lacking literary and political culture, are unable to join the great international humanist community and are turning to Zen.

Goodman asserts that former students of Black Mountain College, an institution oriented toward community and the creative arts — a powerful, and powerfully disaffiliating, combination — are among the pillars of Beat society, alongside former comrades from the armed forces. “pillars of Beat society”; communal origins: BMC and the army. Consequences: The communal spirit of the Beats (shared housing, shared goods, shared culture) would derive in part from BMC.
After sixteen years at Black Mountain College, Albers becomes chairman of the Department of Design at Yale. Consequences: His teaching of color extended beyond BMC

Still fresh from the faculty quarrels at Black Mountain, Albers makes a minimum of administrative duties a condition of accepting the Yale post; the dean, not the chairman, handled administration, and art professors sat on no university committees. Consequences: He keeps complete autonomy over the recruitment of young colleagues (chosen from among his former students) and is the final, often sole, arbiter of admissions

After 25 years of institutional life, the Alberses at last buy a house in a suburban development on a main road, about a mile west of Yale's athletic fields; Anni has to learn to cook; they start from scratch after 16 years at Black Mountain. Living-room furniture: benches upholstered in white Naugahyde taken from the front seat of a 1950s car; a blood-red Cape Cod cottage Consequences: The couple's first owned home, which Albers describes as a young couple starting a new life

Forced to support himself as an itinerant teacher just after leaving Black Mountain in 1949, Albers teaches at the Pratt Institute evening school, keeping the daytime hours for his own work; he says he is becoming a better traveling salesman; he cheerfully accepts the intensity of the courses without assistants. No assistant for the full load of these short courses Consequences: Then the Yale post arrives; he writes that the free life of an artist and the wanderings of an educational globe-trotter are over

The advisory committee, aware that the art program appeared narrow and provincial, chooses Albers as the dynamic leader and spokesman for a perception-based visual education inherited from the Bauhaus, which was to integrate art and architecture with design as the common denominator. Consequences: A new curriculum raising the intellectual process above style and technique

Taking Arnheim by the arm, Albers tells him that when he arrived at Yale the first thing he said was: no more nude women, only squares. the gesture: taking him by the arm Consequences: illustrates his exclusion of the nude from the basic drawing course

Albers transforms Yale's painting program like a tornado: he replaces the basic course with Robert Scott; Gute and Keller (watercolor, portraiture) become isolated; York, seeing the change coming, resigns in May 1950; Rathbone continues an intermediate course reserved for Yale College students. Before Albers: an annual basic course on plaster casts and live models, the tradition of Ingres, portraiture, fresco, egg tempera with gilding. Consequences: Many students of the old system withdraw; the rise of nonobjective painting noted by the student press in February 1951.
Albers accepts a post at Yale, knowing that it is for six years, with mandatory retirement at sixty-eight Consequences: The move from Black Mountain to Yale

Albers's arrival upsets a conservative group attached to the Beaux-Arts tradition. Eisenman, thanks to his leadership and Albers's prestige, assembles a prestigious faculty. Among the guests: Lester Beall, Alexey Brodovitch, Armin Hoffmann, Norman Ives, Leo Lionni, Alvin Lustig, Paul Rand, Bradbury Thompson, Herbert Matter Consequences: Albers's influence judged total (Eisenman) or strong but not day to day (Geismar)

Albers shortens the department's program from five to four years; according to Alfred E. Hammer II, this decision may have been motivated in part by the expected negative reaction of the students: it allowed him to get rid of a class a year earlier.

A year as a visiting professor in several cities, culminating in a permanent post at Yale as chairman of the design department Consequences: There he begins the Homage to the Square and Structural Constellation series, which will occupy him for decades
The design of Albers's fireplace wall in Gropius's Harvard Graduate Center, executed in 1950, remains as a testimony to his Harvard years.

Gropius pushes Harvard to create a basic design course and makes overtures to Albers, who has just resigned from Black Mountain College. Sawyer goes to New York to sound Albers out; Albers accepts Yale. Sawyer supposes that Albers preferred Yale to avoid Gropius's shadow, but Albers in fact never received a formal offer from Harvard. Consequences: Albers chooses Yale.

In the fall of 1950, Albers, in his sixty-second year, begins a new career as chairman of the Department of Design and professor of art at Yale, training a new generation of artists, architects, and educators. 62 at the time of the appointment.

De Kooning carries the summer sessions' model of an artistic community to New York in 1950 by taking part in the founding of the Artists' Club, a gathering devoted to the presentation of avant-garde ideas. Consequences: the Black Mountain model spreads in the New York art world

The critic Clement Greenberg, then in a relationship with the painter Helen Frankenthaler, visits Black Mountain in the summer of 1950; this chance visit contributed to the college's formal posterity. Greenberg had written “The Crisis of the Easel Picture” (1948) two years earlier. Consequences: Greenberg's formalist ideology then dominated the narrative of midcentury art, obscuring the “extraoptical” character of Black Mountain art.
A group exhibition at MoMA.

Amino comes back to teach sculpture; meanwhile his interest has shifted from natural materials to the artificial, from carving to casting, from the intrinsic to the additive. Consequences: He makes innovative sculptures in plastic resin
Recommended by de Kooning, Greenberg teaches there; he credits the students with an impressive intensity but concludes that not much great art came out of Black Mountain (only a few famous names).

When an attempt is made to dismiss Albert William Levi in 1950, M. C. Richards, a well-liked English teacher and poet, is refused the renewal of her appointment despite strong campus support for her teaching.

A meeting followed by their first collaboration on Music of Changes (1951), composed with the help of the I Ching on charts of sounds, durations, and dynamics. Consequences: The beginning of the close Cage-Tudor collaboration in the early 1950s.
The college stops most of its official publications: intertwined causes — the faculty schism, the fall in enrollment after the GI Bill was changed.

Rockburne arrives from Montreal at eighteen, meets her first husband, the printmaking teacher Carroll Williams, becomes pregnant, and has little time left to create; her conversations with Max Dehn will nourish her celebrated painting. he taught her to see mathematics in nature (interview of September 26, 2014)

Stamos takes part in the protest against the Metropolitan Museum (the photograph of the “Irascibles” in Life), has a solo show at the Phillips Collection in Washington, and is invited to teach at Black Mountain for the summer. Consequences: There he paints Beyond the Mountains, Number 1 and The Emperor Plows the Fields.

A summer session teaching painting; he often takes his students to paint on nearby Mount Mitchell; his studio overlooks farmland and mist-veiled mountains. Consequences: A turning point: he abandons literal biomorphic imagery for an abstraction rooted in the perception of nature.
On the way to Yucatán in early 1950, Olson and his common-law wife Constance conceive their daughter Kate. Olson saw Yucatán as a refuge from what was soon to happen in the United States.
Olson and his common-law wife Constance conceive their daughter Kate during the trip to Yucatán. Consequences: The birth of their daughter Kate
Kline has his first solo exhibition at the Egan Gallery in New York the year before Twombly's summer.

Duncan writes the poem “The Song of the Borderguard” as he falls in love with Jess Collins, a nuclear physicist who has just broken with the military-intellectual complex to start over in the San Francisco art scene. Consequences: The poem will be printed as a broadside at Black Mountain in 1952.

Olson (40) and Creeley (24), both at the forefront of their poetic invention, begin to correspond — an epistolary energy that will unite them and lead to the Black Mountain Review. Olson was 40, Creeley 24 Consequences: Collaboration on the review from 1954 on.
Archer edits the collection Five Photographers (Black Mountain College, 1950), containing her text “Photography at Black Mountain College” and Cernovich's text “Even Monkeys Can Take Pictures”.

The couple settles in a working-class Victorian house on Saturn Street; there Asawa establishes a way of working integrated into the rhythms of family life, an orientation she will keep all her life. A flat-file cabinet serving as a makeshift partition, a mattress on the floor as a workstation at kitchen level Consequences: This mode of life-as-work within domesticity becomes her signature as an artist-mother

In the early 1950s, Guermonprez informally mentored Asawa and frequently gave weaving lessons at her home to the children of Asawa, of Lee (Renk), and of Renk — approaches that the Alvarado School Arts Workshop would later take up. Consequences: A model for later school art workshops.
In the early 1950s, Asawa helps Guermonprez prepare seven weaving demonstration panels for the museum. Seven panels.

The wall hanging Leaf Study shown in the de Young's Pond Farm exhibition in 1950; Asawa would have seen it — a piece from the series of “textile graphics” in which Guermonprez painted directly on the warp threads, sometimes with stencils. Painting on the warp, use of stencils.

The first meeting of the two women, 43 years apart; Cunningham offers to photograph the Lanier children, giving rise to baby albums of hybrid status (family snapshots / works of art) Cunningham, born in 1883, trained in pictorialism; Asawa trained in the era of Abstract Expressionism Consequences: Twenty-six years of photographic exchanges until Cunningham's death in 1976

Albert Lanier's employer, the architect Mario Corbett, hires Rondal Partridge to document a house he has designed; Asawa accompanies Lanier and Rondal on the site visit. Consequences: Rondal then suggests that Asawa meet his mother, Imogen Cunningham.
Shortly after they meet, Cunningham visits the young couple with a jar of homemade Satsuma plum jam. A jar of homemade Satsuma plum jam. Consequences: Beginning of a lasting friendship.

Albers leaves Black Mountain to head the new Department of Design of the Yale School of Fine Arts, created from the former departments of Painting and Sculpture. Consequences: Confirms his wish to return to an art-centered program; he adds courses in Basic Design, Elementary Drawing, and Color

The college tries to run entirely on student fees, with no endowment or outside contributions; Goodman details its costs and financial organization. Total fees per student: $1,000 to $1,600 (tuition plus room and board); tuition estimated at $700, about half that of Columbia or Cornell that year; 18 teachers for 100 students; faculty salaries from $600 to about $2,000 a year according to family needs, plus health insurance, food, and housing. Consequences: Costs come close to the academic-guild model Goodman describes, but with an entirely different distribution: property owned by the faculty, a plant largely built by students and teachers, and everyone taking part in the work program.

In a school costing $450 per child, with parents as volunteer teachers, the teachers and parent-teachers oust the founding headmaster, run the school as a communal anarchy in which small children have an equal vote, then return to a headmaster with limited authority. $450 per child; 50 children; 3 paid full-time instructors plus the equivalent of 5 volunteer teachers among the parents. Consequences: Despite the instability, the children were exposed to many attentive and learned adults, the chief advantage in Goodman's view.

Married in the spring; summer spent with Susan's family at their house on Outer Island, Connecticut; back in New York, an apartment on the Upper West Side; freelance window displays for Bonwit Teller and Tiffany. Apartment on the West Side, in the 90s (streets)

Still and Parsons come to choose works for an exhibition; by the opening a few months later, Rauschenberg has repainted the selected pictures dozens of times on an entirely different concept. He recalls being naive and excited, and Betty was surprised. Consequences: The dealer is surprised

In the fall of 1950 (the text places the selection in 1951), they boldly walk into Betty Parsons's gallery carrying as many paintings as they can: a religious series (Garden of Eden, Crucifixion and Reflection, Trinity); Kantor had advised him to approach Parsons; he goes in shyly and with great apprehension. Canvases carried by hand; he had already shown his blueprints in a Life feature (“Speaking of Pictures”) and dressed windows for Eugene Moore at Bonwit Teller; Blueprint: Photogram for Mural Decoration was selected in the spring of 1951 for “Abstraction in Photography” at MoMA Consequences: After a moment of surprise, Parsons offers him a show

After the Parsons show and the Ninth Street Show organized by The Club, he and Weil return to Black Mountain that summer, bringing their newborn, Christopher. Ninth Street Show, “Today's Self-Styled School of New York”

Rauschenberg lays objects (often a woman's body, sometimes with flowers and shells) on blueprint paper exposed to the sun, in the manner of Man Ray's rayographs. Only one known work survives, the Nude Blueprint. A body lying directly on the paper, life-size, with differences in pressure and light leaks creating a ghostly image Consequences: Anticipates the silhouette in Wager (1957-59) and the X-ray in Visual Autobiography; photograph incorporated into Odalisk (1955-58)

The “Projective Verse” manifesto is a pastiche of letters written to the poet Robert Creeley; it calls for a spontaneity grounded in the breath. Consequences: Poetic charter of the Black Mountain school
Olson begins his magnum opus, shaped as a series of epistles, drawing on found materials (logbooks, captains' letters) and invoking the history of the port of Gloucester.
M.C. Richards stages the Cocteau play in the round.

After an American tour two years earlier, Leach publishes a severe analysis of American pottery in Craft Horizons. Craft Horizons, fall 1950. Consequences: Background tension for the 1952 seminar and for Wildenhain's response.

After an American trip two years earlier, Leach publishes in Craft Horizons (fall 1950) a scathing analysis of American pottery: Americans have many roots but no taproot, hence pots that follow undigested fashions; he is glad to have been born into an old culture whose sap still flows from a deep root, giving a sense of form, pattern, and color below the level of intellectualization. Publication: Craft Horizons, fall 1950, “American Impressions.” Consequences: Very mixed responses: he is blamed for belittling Native American traditions and ignoring the vernacular traditions he dislikes; his own pots are called stifling, heavy, mid-Victorian, and incredibly dull.

In the 1950s, on an American tour, Rosanjin throws a bowl until it collapses; he then makes thick coils of clay to hold it up and presents this extraordinary fall to his horrified audience of American potters to be admired. Told by M.C. Richards in Centering. Thick coils of clay used as props. Consequences: A display of exploratory, improvised pottery, the very opposite of American academicism.

Weil and Rauschenberg marry in the spring of 1950 and spend the summer on Outer Island, where they discover the possibilities of the blueprint process and its artistically impersonal results. They make the first life-size blueprint image of a human figure (Weil's six-year-old brother). About twelve images survive; Weil writes the poetic titles, e.g., “Suspended Shadow Declared Eternal by the Death of Time”; a tradition going back to William Fox Talbot's “photogenic drawings” (1835); Weil's grandmother had printed a small blueprint of herself as a child in her father's architectural office; as a child, she had experimented with the process using leaves and flowers Consequences: Key documents of modernism, foreshadowing their taste for collaboration
Nemyni, who studied physics with Max Dehn, leaves the college for Princeton around 1950; saying goodbye is both happy and sad.

A gay student, a former Moderator before Dan, sitting outside with a group, announces that a new faculty member arriving in the fall is gay. Asked how he knows, he pretends to be shocked, promises to prove it, and does. Consequences: Opening of the school's homosexual period

In the fall of 1950 a new pottery student arrives, also gay, nicknamed Kitty; after the Paul Goodman summer, several boys (and the girls too) take an interest in him, as if overnight. Consequences: New distinctions within the student body; the school adjusts to itself

Dawson's first year (1949-1950): Olson commutes from Washington, D.C., and begins teaching in the fall of 1950. He reads students' manuscripts aloud before any discussion; awkward at first, he embarrasses himself by attributing to Mary a poem written by Mark, and Mary sharply corrects him (a memory still vivid in 1989-1990; some people have long memories).
In the late spring of 1950, Dawson writes a story titled “Father,” later published in The Black Mountain College Review, edited by M.C. (Mary Caroline Richards).
Dawson writes Father in the late spring of 1950; it later appears in The Black Mountain College Review, edited by M.C. Richards. Consequences: Publication of his first recognized piece.

Dawson, twenty, reads his newly written story Father to the assembled students and teachers, scared to death, and slips away amid unexpected applause to let someone else read. Reading aloud, unexpected applause. Consequences: The next day, a compliment from Mary, who uses the word “writer.”

The day after the reading, Mary compliments Dawson in a soft voice full of surprise and admiration and calls him a “writer.” Window by the sink, near the stoves and the back entrance. Consequences: An unforgettable memory that underlies Mary's suggestion a year later.

Toward the end of his first year, a wart appears on top of Dawson's right wrist; he scratches it out of habit, sometimes until it bleeds. Wart on top of the right wrist Consequences: Becomes an obsessive motif until it disappears in 1952

Laughing, Corny ties a thread around the wart and sprinkles it with dirt; they chant “Go away wart” three times with their eyes closed, then bury the thread in a small hole; she announces a two-week wait. Two weeks later the thread has vanished: the spell has partly failed, and they roar with laughter. A thread about six inches long, a small covered hole, a few pebbles placed around it by Dawson Consequences: The wart stays; Dawson gets rid of it himself in September 1952

Dawson begs an art teacher to hit him; the man finally does, Dawson cries, and the teacher walks out of the kitchen in disgust; Corny, who saw it, has pain in her eyes. Consequences: Corny gives him a paper cup of homemade peach brandy and tells him to take care of himself

Spring 1950: Olson dreams he is standing in a street in broad daylight in Washington and sees a Soviet bomber in the sky carrying the Bomb; he wakes up frightened and tells the dream that same morning on the porch, wide eyes fixed beyond the lake. Bright daylight; a gaze drilled into space Consequences: Dawson reads it as an anxiety dream foretelling his future

Stoehr's first meeting with Goodman; family income under $1,000 a year. Annual income under $1,000; rent of $26 a month for four or five rooms above a paint store, Ninth Avenue, Manhattan; bookshelves made of old orange crates

May: protests with other artists against the selections for “American Painting Today, 1950” at the Met; summer: chosen by Barr for the 25th Venice Biennale, his first show abroad; begins Woman I; fall: visiting critic in painting at Yale, at Josef Albers's invitation.

Named chairman of the Department of Design at Yale, he makes four machine-engraved brass prints, his first Structural Constellations, and the same year begins the Homages to the Square, at 61. 4 engravings on brass; age 61 Consequences: Twenty-seven years of relentless work on these two bodies of work
